It depends on what you’re missing. If you don’t have a resume, or you want the page designed for you, you need a builder: Kickresume, Rezi, Enhancv, and Teal all do that, free with limits and by subscription for the rest. If you have a resume and you’re tailoring it to many postings, you need a keyword scanner: Jobscan, or the matching inside Teal and Rezi. If you want it written for you, TopResume. If you have a resume and want to know what a recruiter would question before you send it, you need a recruiter’s read, and that is what the report is.

The report’s limits, so you can weigh it fairly: it reads the words we pull from your file, not the design, and it is AI applying a recruiter’s criteria, not a person reading your resume. It gives no keyword score and no interview odds, and it won’t build, design, or track anything. In November 2026 we ran one resume through five of these tools and ours; each of those pages says what came back, under “How we compare”. It was one resume, one role, one day, so these pages still mostly compare what each tool sells. The research behind the read is linked where it applies:
Most people need one builder or none, a scanner only if they apply in volume, and one honest read of the resume before it goes out. The read is free here.
You want the page designed.
Real leverage. In our experience, a competing offer is the most reliable way to move a number, so it's worth finishing other processes. Never invent one.
On the offer call, thank them and ask questions

One of five bands, with a line on what it means, and the number beside it. The top one, Ready to send, is earned: it means no line on the page needs work. The band is what a recruiter would do with the resume after one pass.

Every line a recruiter trips on gets a card: the line as written, what they can’t tell from it, an example with the blanks for you to fill, and the question that fills them. Nothing in an example is invented; the facts are your resume’s or yours.

I'm applying for [job title] at [company]. Here's the posting: [paste the link or the text]. I've attached my LinkedIn connections (Connections.csv) and my resume. 1. List everyone in the file whose Company is [company], with their name, position, and the date we connected. Put anyone whose title sounds close to this role or its team first. 2. Don't guess how well I know anyone. After the list, ask me which of these people I know and how. 3. For each person I pick, draft a short message I could send on LinkedIn. Use only facts from my resume and what I tell you about how we know each other. Don't invent shared history, praise, or details about their work. 4. Each message should say how we know each other in one line, name the role with the link, ask whether they'd be comfortable referring me, offer to send a few sentences they can paste into the referral form, and make it easy to say no. Write it the way I'd message a former colleague: warm, plain, and short enough to read on a phone, with no buzzwords.
which job ads you see, whether you’re eligible, and how you reach a person
Your report is a recruiter's read of the page, not an ATS score. It works from the text we pull from your file, so it can't tell you how a particular employer's software or filters will treat it.

every gap, pivot, or short stint raises a question. Answer it on the page before the reader answers it for you.

If a gap or a pivot is the question your resume leaves open, the write-up says so in plain words, and the gap gets a card of its own: an honest dated line with the blank for what you were doing, never a story invented for you.
Say what changed, how you measured it, and what you did to get there
Use titles, headings, and dates a reader recognizes.

Your report opens with a recruiter’s write-up: what your resume says first, in plain words. Where your role, scope, or results are unclear, the line gets a card, in the order a recruiter hits it. It can’t tell you how long anyone will look.
Make your evidence easy to inspect, too: clear role context, specific ownership, supportable outcomes, and no claims you can't defend. That is the part of the page a reader weighs:

Your report reads your resume, not your LinkedIn profile. It cards each line a recruiter trips on, in the order they hit it, and asks for what's missing instead of inventing it. Fix the resume, then carry the same plain language over to your profile.
When a line says what you did but not what changed, it gets a card. We'll ask for the result or the scale. We won't invent one for you.
No study we know of isolates a quantified bullet against a duty-style one. What the research does show is how recruiters use what's on the page.
It tested help with wording on short profiles, not adding results, but it shows that how clearly a profile reads can change outcomes.

Your report won't tell you what to ask for. It reads your resume: the write-up says what it says first, and each line a recruiter trips on gets a card that asks for what's missing instead of inventing it.

It also can't say whether spelling matters more than content: the study kept the content the same and changed only the spelling. What it shows is that repeated errors cost points even when the experience on the page is identical. It fits what a much larger experiment found when only the wording changed:
Your report isn't a spell-checker. It cards the lines a recruiter trips on, in the order they hit them. Run a spell-check last, after you've worked through the cards.
When a line hides your part or the result, it gets a card that asks for them. Filling it gives you the headline of a story you can tell, and the score weighs how easy it is to follow what you did.

Run the free report before you buy a rewrite, so you know what the writer has to fix and what facts to put in the intake. Run it again on the draft that comes back, and check that the lines it carded the first time are off the list.

Build and track in Teal, then export the resume you plan to send and run it through the free report before it goes out. If the report cards a line, fix it in Teal and export again.

Ours led with the resume’s own numbers, put one line first with the line it came from, and questioned a “300% reduction in time to hire” as a figure that can’t be right. Thirty-six seconds without the posting, a minute and a half with it, and no line misread. One resume, one role, one day, on the report as it ran then; the report now cards every line a recruiter trips on, not one.
What it won’t do: design the page, write a resume from a job title, or build you a website.

: Free at $0 with four basic resume templates, four matching cover letter templates, one basic website template, 20,000 pre-written phrases, 1,500 resume examples, and unlimited downloads; Monthly at $24; Quarterly at $54 every three months, shown as $18 a month; and Yearly at $96 every twelve months, shown as $8 a month and marked as a 25% saving. The paid plans share one feature list: 40 resume and 40 cover letter templates, all colors and typefaces, the AI Writer, the ATS Resume Checker, Career Map, LinkedIn and PDF import, the mobile apps, seven personal website templates, priority support, and a 14-day money-back guarantee. A human grammar correction is $30 per resume. Students who verify with ISIC, ITIC, or UNiDAYS get Premium free.
Pricing (plans, prices, and what each includes)

: Free at $0 with one resume, one AI interview, three PDF downloads, the standard templates, and the AI writer and editor, with the Rezi Score, keyword targeting, and real-time analysis limited; Pro at $29 a month with unlimited resumes, interviews, and downloads, all templates, the full score and keyword targeting, Word and Google Drive export, and one expert resume review a month; a Lifetime plan at $149 for one payment, described as all features; and Enterprise at $99 a month per 200 users. The page’s title says all plans include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

Build in Rezi if the live score keeps you writing, then export the PDF and run the free report before it goes out. Where the score says you’re done and the report cards a line, trust the card: it’s the question a recruiter would ask.

doesn’t touch the design. It reads the words on the resume you have the way a recruiter would, free for the first report. If the look of the page is what you’re after, Enhancv is built for that. If you want to know whether the words hold up, start here.

Enhancv is a resume builder for people who want the page to look designed: hundreds of templates, drag-and-drop sections, and content suggestions, free for seven days with its branding on the PDF, then from $16.50 a month on a six-month plan.
What it won’t do: design the page, offer templates, or export a styled resume. The PDF you can download is the report.

OpenAI generates reports and smooths the revised lines you build from your answers, Supabase handles auth and database storage, Stripe handles billing, Vercel provides hosting and basic page statistics, Sentry handles error and performance monitoring, and Mixpanel handles optional product analytics after you allow it. Vercel's page statistics use no cookies: they record the page, the referring site, approximate location, and device and browser type, identify a visit only by a hash that is discarded after 24 hours, and never include report ids or other private parts of a page address. Upstash provides shared rate limiting and short-lived idempotency storage. Inngest coordinates background account-export jobs when you request one. Resend delivers authentication email and receives public support mail; support messages and attachments are forwarded to and handled in Google (Gmail). Stripe manages card data on its systems. We never have access to it.

Use Privacy choices in the footer to allow or decline optional analytics. Declining also stops Vercel's page statistics in this browser, as does a Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control signal. Declining does not affect your report or account. We remember your choice in this browser. Withdrawing permission stops future analytics and clears its local identifiers and queued events; it does not delete events already received by Mixpanel. Essential storage still supports sign-in, free-report eligibility, and your privacy choice. You can delete individual reports from Reports. In Settings, you can export your account data or permanently delete your account. Account deletion removes user-owned product data from RIYP's application database and cancels any legacy RIYP subscription we can verify. Stripe may retain payment records, and RIYP keeps narrowly scoped deletion and billing-reversal records when needed to prevent restored access, investigate fraud, meet accounting obligations, or comply with law. We don't sell personal data, and anonymous history is not silently attached to an account.
